titel: Interest rates as the basis of valuation
kurz: Every asset price is a discounted stream of payments, and the risk-free rate is part of every one of these discount calculations.

bloecke.md:
On 18 September 2026 the ten-year German federal bond yields 3.52% and the thirty-year 3.83%, while the ten-year US Treasury yielded 4.94% the day before. These figures do not only concern bond buyers. They enter every share valuation and every property calculation as the denominator. Indirectly, they also affect pension provisions in company balance sheets, which are discounted under IFRS using yields on high-quality corporate bonds and under the HGB (Commercial Code) using the average market interest rate of the past ten years as determined by the Bundesbank.

This is because an asset is the sum of its future payments, each discounted to today. If the discount rate rises, the present value falls, even if nothing about the payments themselves changes. The risk-free rate is the lower limit of every discount rate because it describes the alternative. Anyone who buys a risky investment forgoes the government bond of the same maturity and currency and demands a higher return in exchange.

For the companies surveyed from Germany, Austria and Switzerland, the study reports 9.7% as the average cost of equity used in practice and 8.5% as the weighted average cost of capital (WACC).

bloecke.md:
## Choosing the risk-free rate

In German valuation practice under the standard of the IDW (Institute of Public Auditors in Germany), the [[Risk-free base rate (Basiszins)|risk-free base rate (Basiszins)]] is not read off the current daily yield. It is derived from the Bundesbank's yield curve estimated with the Svensson method, smoothed over three months and rounded to 0.25 percentage points. The convention deliberately follows the market with a delay so that a company's value does not track every short-term movement in interest rates. As of 1 September 2026, this produced a base rate of 3.75% (3.63% unrounded). Because the yields on long maturities are also included, it is above the ten-year Bund yield (3.52% on 18 September 2026). The 2.5% from the KPMG study 2025 in the formula example above is the average that the companies surveyed used at the time.

Whether the chosen rate fits the valuation depends on three rules.

- The currency must match. Cash flows in euros are discounted with a euro curve, not with the US Treasury yield. The difference of 1.42 percentage points in mid-September 2026 is not a premium; it results from the different currency.
- The maturity must fit. A company that will continue operating indefinitely needs the long end of the curve. The ECB deposit facility rate of 2.50% is a price for overnight money and unsuitable as a reference for valuations.
- Nominal and real figures must not be mixed. Nominal cash flows go with nominal interest rates. The real yield on ten-year US inflation-linked bonds was 2.61% on 17 September 2026. If real cash flows are discounted at 4.94%, inflation is deducted twice.

## Shares as long-dated securities

The interest rate sensitivity of a bond is measured by its duration, which was covered in the previous lessons. The same concept can be applied to shares, and the result explains why in 2022 shares whose profits lie far in the future lost more than others.

In the Gordon growth model, the value of a payment that grows forever at `g` is `V = CF₁ / (r − g)`. Differentiating this expression with respect to `r` gives a closed-form formula for the present-value-weighted average period for which capital is tied up, the [[Equity duration|equity duration]].

bloecke.erklaerung: Macaulay duration of a perpetually growing stream of payments. The closer the growth rate is to the discount rate, the larger the proportion of the equity value that comes from distant payments, and the more strongly the price reacts to changes in interest rates.
bloecke.beispiel: With r = 8% and g = 2%, that is 18.0 years; with g = 4%, as much as 27.0 years. A ten-year German federal bond with a 2.5% coupon has a Macaulay duration of 8.9 years at a market yield of 3.52%, the thirty-year bond one of 20.4 years.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation of Macaulay duration using the Gordon model at a discount rate of 8%, broken down by assumed perpetual growth; the reference line shows the Macaulay duration of a ten-year German federal bond.

bloecke.titel: Interest rate sensitivity of the stock market
bloecke.md: The stock market's sensitivity to interest rates is not due to companies taking out loans. The reason is that a share is a stream of payments with a duration of 15 to 40 years, two to four times that of a ten-year bond. This makes the long-term interest rate the single most important number for the stock market, even for investors who never own a bond.

The company “Mature Payer” distributes 100 units of free cash flow a year starting now and grows forever at 2%.

The company “Late Bloomer” earns nothing distributable for five years, pays out around 25.6 units from year 6, increases this by 25% a year for nine years until year 15 and then also grows at 2%.

At a discount rate of 5.79%, both are worth exactly 2,639 units, so they would be indistinguishable in the market. Their durations, however, differ considerably: 27.9 versus 37.8 years.

At the beginning of 2022 the ten-year Bund yielded −0.21%, at the end of 2022 +2.53%, a rise of 274 basis points. If the risk premium is held constant at 6.0 percentage points, the discount rate rises from 5.79% to 8.53%.

- Mature Payer: 2,639 → 1,531, that is −42.0%
- Late Bloomer: 2,639 → 1,193, that is −54.8%

The valuation losses are in almost exactly the same ratio as the durations (37.8 / 27.9 = 1.35 compared with 54.8 / 42.0 = 1.30). Neither business model has changed and no forecast has been lowered; the only thing that has risen is the discount rate in the denominator.

bloecke.titel: Value of the example companies at different discount rates
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation based on the present value principle; value of the two example companies, indexed to 100 at the starting rate of 5.79%, at which both are deliberately equally expensive.

bloecke.md:
## 2022 and the limits of the model

In 2022 the yield on two-year German federal bonds rose by 325 basis points, that on ten-year bonds by 274. Prices reacted as duration would lead you to expect. Shares whose profits are expected far in the future lost more than shares with earlier profits.

The illustrative calculation above does exaggerate, however. It gives −42% for Mature Payer, whereas the S&P 500 lost 19.44% in 2022 on a price basis and 18.11% on a total return basis. The simple model lacks two effects. First, nominal profits grew with inflation. If interest rates rise because of higher expected inflation, `g` rises too, and `r − g` changes less than `r`. Second, the risk premium is not constant. It shrank while the risk-free rate rose. This is why the expected total return on equities remains more stable across cycles than the movement in interest rates suggests.

bloecke.unter: Nasdaq-100 and S&P 500 as price indices, DAX as a performance index including dividends; the series are therefore not fully comparable, but the ranking by the weight of growth companies is clear.

bloecke.md:
The assumption “interest rates rise by one point, so my discount rate rises by one point” only holds if the risk premium and growth expectations remain unchanged. In practice, the effect depends on why interest rates are rising.

- If the real interest rate rises, for example because the central bank tightens policy without inflation expectations increasing, valuations take the full hit.
- If interest rates rise only because expected inflation increases, nominal cash flows grow as well. A company with pricing power then loses little or nothing.

The market itself provides the split into real interest rate and inflation expectations. The nominal yield minus the real yield on indexed bonds gives break-even inflation, in the US on 17 September 2026: 4.94% minus 2.61% ≈ 2.33%.

## The Fed model and its weaknesses

Edward Yardeni coined the term in 1997, after a chart in the Fed's Humphrey-Hawkins report had placed the earnings yield of the S&P 500 next to the yield on ten-year Treasuries. The rule is simple. If the earnings yield (earnings divided by price, the inverse of the P/E ratio) is above the bond yield, equities are considered cheap; if it is below, they are considered expensive.

At present the model's verdict is clear-cut. That is a reason to examine the model thoroughly instead of simply following it.

bloecke.md:
First, the model compares a real quantity with a nominal one. The earnings on which the earnings yield is based grow with inflation; the coupon of a bond does not. In 2003 Cliff Asness described this, under the title “Fight the Fed Model”, as money illusion in the sense of Modigliani and Cohn. In practice, investors set P/E ratios according to nominal interest rates and are therefore systematically wrong.

Second, the model implicitly assumes that there is no equity risk premium and that earnings do not grow. Both are obviously untrue.

Third, the model has no predictive power. An analysis by Ned Davis Research (2018) found a coefficient of determination of 0.5% for future returns, compared with 56.3% for the simple P/E ratio and 67.2% for the price-to-sales ratio. Yardeni himself later admitted that the relationship stopped working practically from the moment it was discovered.

As a description, the model remains useful. It shows how investors process interest rates, but not what a share is worth.

## Estimates of the equity risk premium

Above the risk-free rate lies the equity risk premium. There is no market quotation for it, only estimation methods whose results are far apart.

The historically realised premium is derived from past returns. From 1928 to 2025 the S&P 500 returned 10.02% a year in nominal terms (geometric, including dividends), and thus 6.65 percentage points more than the money market. The objection is that realised returns need not correspond to expected returns. Part of this premium arose from a rise in valuations that cannot be repeated.

For the [[Implied equity risk premium|implied equity risk premium]], Damodaran works back from the current index level and expected distributions to the return the market is pricing in. At the beginning of September 2026 this is 4.14% above a risk-free rate of 4.75%, so the expected total return is around 8.9%. For Germany, Damodaran gives a total equity risk premium of 4.23% as of January 2026, with a country risk premium of zero.

Then there is the practice of expert valuation reports. Since September 2025 the IDW has recommended 5.25 to 6.75 percentage points before personal taxes for Germany (previously 6.0 to 8.0), and KPMG's survey finds 6.7%. The gap of around one to two and a half percentage points to the implied estimate is not a calculation error. It is due to different methods. Besides implied returns, the IDW also takes historical returns and premiums into account, whereas the implied estimate is based solely on the current price level. When reading a valuation, you should therefore know which method it follows.

bloecke.titel: Fair P/E ratio by discount rate and growth
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation using the Gordon model with full payout, where P/E = 1 / (r − g); just one percentage point more interest or less growth shifts the fair P/E ratio by many times the precision that most price targets claim.

bloecke.titel: The false precision of price targets
bloecke.md: With r = 6% and g = 4%, the heatmap shows a fair P/E ratio of 50; with r = 8% and g = 2%, one of 16.7. Two defensible sets of parameters are thus a factor of three apart. For this reason a DCF calculation does not deliver an exact value. It shows which assumptions fit a price. It therefore makes more sense to work backwards and ask which `r` and which `g` the current price implies.

1. The interest rate must match the stream of payments. Both need the same currency and the same maturity, and they must be either both nominal or both real.
2. The growth rate must be below the discount rate, because `g ≥ r` produces an infinite value. As a perpetual rate, anything above the economy's nominal trend growth is not sustainable.
3. The calculation can be reversed by solving for `r` instead of specifying `r`. The return priced in is a more meaningful number than any price target.

bloecke.titel: Key interest rate and long-term interest rate
bloecke.md: The ECB deposit facility rate steers the terms for instant-access savings. It was 2.00% in June 2025, 2.25% in June 2026 and has been 2.50% since 16 September 2026. For valuations, what counts is the long end, which is determined by expected future short-term interest rates and a term premium. A rise in the key interest rate can therefore even lower the long-term interest rate if the market sees it as an effective way of fighting inflation. A valuation model that hinges on key interest rate decisions relies on the wrong number.

mitnehmen: The risk-free rate does not only affect bonds, because it is a term in every cost of capital and therefore sits in the denominator of every asset price.
At 15 to 40 years, shares have the longest duration of all common investments and therefore react more strongly to changes in interest rates than most bonds.
The further in the future a company's payments lie, the greater the valuation loss when interest rates rise; this mechanism lies behind the 2022 slump in the shares of growth companies.
What matters is why interest rates rise, because a higher real interest rate hits valuations in full, whereas higher inflation expectations also raise nominal growth.
The Fed model describes how investors process interest rates, but not what a share is worth; it compares a real quantity with a nominal one and has no predictive power.

begriffe.text: The risk-free rate used in valuation practice. In Germany, by IDW convention, it is derived from the Bundesbank's yield curve estimated with the Svensson method, smoothed and rounded to 0.25 percentage points. This is why it differs from the current daily yield.

Present-value-weighted average period for which capital is tied up in a share's expected payments. In the Gordon model, D = (1+r)/(r−g). Typical values are 15 to 40 years, considerably more than for most bonds.

The excess return over the risk-free rate that can be backed out from the current price level and expected distributions. It is the counterpart to the historically realised premium. The two methods currently produce values that are several percentage points apart.

Rule of thumb that compares the earnings yield of the stock index with the yield on ten-year government bonds. Edward Yardeni gave it its name in 1997. It is theoretically questionable because it compares a real quantity with a nominal one, and it has no demonstrable predictive power.
Difference between the nominal yield on a government bond and the real yield on an inflation-linked bond of the same maturity. It shows what inflation the market is pricing in over that period.
